claims.text: High-temperature structural and chemical stability of multi-element, near-equiatomic nanoparticles is governed by formation of a single-phase solid solution.
Inhibiting precursor mobility during nanoparticle formation favors formation of a single-phase solid solution.
Stochastic principles govern formation of the high-entropy-alloy nanoparticles.
With limited free-atom mobility, increasing the number of atom types makes random-alloy formation more likely.
The presence of multiple elements with similar atomic radii favors formation of a single-phase solid solution.
Elements with a lower heat of formation favor formation of a single-phase solid solution.
A single-phase solid solution will improve nanoparticle structural stability during high-temperature service.
A single-phase solid solution will improve nanoparticle chemical stability during high-temperature service.
Combined in situ X-ray powder diffraction and multi-edge X-ray absorption spectroscopy can investigate high-entropy-alloy nanoparticle formation.
The proposed in situ diffraction and absorption measurements can establish nanoparticle stabilization throughout the stated high-temperature service ranges.
The relevant catalytic service range is 773–1173 K.
The relevant thermoelectric service range is 473–1923 K.
The proposed formation and stabilization mechanism applies to nanoparticles with low noble-metal content.
The exact mechanisms of single-phase formation and the effects of multiple elements on nanoparticle stability are not fully understood.
Failure to form a single-phase solid solution under the specified conditions would falsify the hypothesis.
